source_text: Δημιουργὸν τῶν πάντων τιθέμενος αὐτὸν τὸ τοῦ Λόγου ὄνομα κατηγορεῖ αὐτοῦ. ἐπεὶ γὰρ ὡς ἐπίπαν πᾶσα δημιουργία ἤρτηται λόγου, οὐκ ἄλλως ἔδει αὐτὸν τῶν πάντων δηλῶσαι ὄντα ποιητὴν ἔχουσιν (αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἕξις μετὰ ἀδόλου λόγου ποιητική), ὁ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱός, οὐκ ἄλλος ὢς ἢ σοφίας καὶ τέχνης δημιουργός, εἰκότως λόγος ὀνομάζεται. οὐ γὰρ ἄλλη τις ὢν οὐσία παρὰ τὸν λόγου δι᾿ αὐτοῦ ποιεὶ τὰ ὄντα, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ ποιῶν, θεὸς ὢν λόγος. εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ ὁ λόγος οὗτος, θεὸς ὢν κατ’ οὐσίαν καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο θεοῦ υἱὸς ὑπάρχων, τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίας χάριν ἄνθρωπος γεγένηται, »Σὰρξ« ὁ λόγος ὠνομάσθη. καὶ ἐπεί τινες τῆς ὀρθῆς πίστεως ἐκπεσόντες οἴονται ἀπὸ τότε αὐτὸν μόνον εἶναι ἀφ’ οὑ ἐκ τῆς παρθένου ἄνθρωπος γεγονὼς προῆλθεν, ὀρθότατα πρὸς τοὺς τοιούτους ὁ θεολόγος γράφει τὸ »Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος« καὶ καταλλήλως τοῖς ῥήμασι χρησάμενος, τῷ μὲν »Ἐγένετο« ἐπὶ τῆς σαρκὸς, τῷ δὲ »Ἦν« ἐπὶ τῆς θεότητος αὐτοῦ σημαίνει]. καὶ ἦν μὲν κυριώτερον ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου τὸ »Ἔστιν« εἰπεῖν· ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ πρὸς διαφορὰν τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως γενομένης ἔν τινι καιρῷ ἐδήλου τὴν ὓπαρξιν τοῦ λόγου, ἀντὶ τοῦ »Ἔστιν« τῷ »Ἦν« ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς κέχρηται. τῶν δὲ ῥημάτων τὰς κυρίας σημασίας ἐκλαμβάνειν οὐ δεῖ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀιδίων· ὅτε μὲν γὰρ τὰ σημαινόμενα ὑπὸ τούτων χρόνῳ συμμετρουμένην ἔχει τὴν ὕπαρξιν, ὡς τὸ Ἦν τὸ μηκέτ’ ὄν, ἀλλά ποτε ὁμοίως τὸ Ἔστι δηλοῖ τὸ νῦν ὑπάρχον, ὡς τὸ Ἔσται τὸ μέλλον ὑπάρξαι]].
thought_title: Why the Son Is Called Word and Flesh
orientation: Origen opens his comment on John by explaining why the Son is called Word as creator and flesh as man for human salvation.
pass_a_gloss: Placing him as maker of all things he predicates of him the name of the Word. For since for the most part every creation hangs from word, it was needful not otherwise to show him being maker of all things having this is a productive state with guileless word, and the son of God, being no other than maker of Wisdom and craft, is reasonably named Word. For being no other substance besides the word he makes the things that are through it, but he himself is the one making, being God Word. Next since this Word, being God in substance and being this very thing son of God, has become man for the sake of the salvation of men, the Word was named flesh. And since some having fallen from the right faith suppose him to be only from then from when having become man from the virgin he came forth, most rightly against such people the theologian writes the In beginning was the Word and having used the verbs fittingly, by the Became on the one hand he signifies concerning the flesh, by the Was on the other hand concerning his divinity. And it would have been more proper to say the Is concerning the Word of God. But since for distinction from the becoming man that happened at some time he was declaring the existence of the Word, instead of the Is the evangelist has used the Was. But one must not take the proper meanings of the verbs upon eternal things. For when the things signified by them have existence measured by time, as the Was signifies the not still being thing, but at some time, likewise the Is signifies the now existing thing, as the Will be signifies the about to exist thing.

choices.why: brief fixes Word for Λόγος in this creator sense
brief fixes flesh for Σὰρξ as incarnate state
keeps verb force to show eternal being set against timed becoming
source only limits proper tense senses here and never adds beyond tense claim

bible_refs.note: quoted source words Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος

pass_b_english: John presents him as the maker of all things, and so he gives him the name Word. As a rule, every act of craftsmanship depends on reason, so there was no other way to show that he is the maker of all, for craft is a productive state guided by sound reason. The Son of God is himself none other than a craftsman working with wisdom and skill, and so he is fittingly called Word. He does not make existing things through the Word as though he were a different being from the Word. He himself is the one who makes them, since he is God, the Word.

Since this Word, who is God in being and who is himself the Son of God, became man for the salvation of men, the Word was called "flesh." Some have fallen from true faith, and they think he exists only from the moment when he came forth as man from the Virgin. Against people who think this, John the Evangelist writes most rightly, "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1). John uses the verbs with exact fitness, "became" for the flesh and "was" for his divinity.

"Is" would have been the more exact word for the Word of God. But John was declaring the existence of the Word in distinction from the becoming man that happened at a particular time, so the Evangelist used "was" instead of "is." Yet we must not take the ordinary meanings of such verbs when they are used of eternal things. Those meanings apply when what is meant has an existence measured by time: "was" means what no longer exists but once did, "is" likewise means what exists now, and "will be" means what is yet to exist.
notes: Parenthesis with ἔχουσιν and ἕξις is ungrammatical in copy and closing brackets look like catena marks. Gloss keeps what stands without filling sense. Also ὢς reads for expected ὢν and παρὰ τὸν λόγου is unclear in case.

problems.quote: The Son of God is himself none other than the maker of Wisdom and skill
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἄλλος ὢν ἢ σοφίας καὶ τέχνης δημιουργός
problems.why: The Greek means a craftsman of wisdom and skill, a wise and skilled maker. 'Maker of Wisdom' says the Son created Wisdom, and Wisdom is the Son himself.
problems.fix: The Son of God is none other than a craftsman working with wisdom and skill

problems.quote: Origen presents him as the maker of all things, and so he gives him the name Word.
problems.source_quote: Δημιουργὸν τῶν πάντων τιθέμενος αὐτὸν τὸ τοῦ Λόγου ὄνομα κατηγορεῖ αὐτοῦ.
problems.why: The subject is the Evangelist, John, who calls him the Word. Origen is the author of this comment, not the one naming the Word.
problems.fix: Since John presents him as the maker of all things, he gives him the name Word.
problems.ruling: τιθέμενος/κατηγορεῖ imply John predicates Logos; not Origen naming him.

problems.quote: Nearly every created thing depends on Word
problems.source_quote: ὡς ἐπίπαν πᾶσα δημιουργία ἤρτηται λόγου
problems.why: This states a general rule: all craftsmanship depends on reason. The English turns it into a claim about created things depending on the divine Word, which breaks the argument.
problems.fix: As a rule, every act of craftsmanship depends on reason (logos)
problems.ruling: πᾶσα δημιουργία ἤρτηται λόγου is craft on reason, not creatures on the Logos.

problems.quote: Origen says the Word was called "flesh."
problems.why: Origen is the author of this text, yet the English names him in the third person. Nothing in the source says 'Origen says', and the insertion confuses who is speaking.
problems.ruling: Source: «Σὰρξ ὁ λόγος ὠνομάσθη» only; no «Origen says»—invents speaker, misleads on voice.

problems.quote: holding as he does a productive state united with blameless Word
problems.source_quote: (αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἕξις μετὰ ἀδόλου λόγου ποιητική)
problems.why: This parenthesis defines craft as a productive state guided by sound reason. Capitalizing 'Word' turns it into a claim about the divine Word and misreads general reason.
problems.fix: for craft is a productive state guided by sound reason
problems.ruling: Parenthesis defines ποιητική ἕξις; μετὰ ἀδόλου λόγου is craft «reason», not capitalized divine Logos.
